grounding_report.claim: Gradient boosted decision trees (GBDT) are a workhorse for tabular data, but they have a dirty secret: categorical features.
Most implementations force you to preprocess categories into numbers — one-hot encoding, label encoding, or target statistics — before training.
One-hot explodes with high-cardinality columns.
Label encoding imposes an arbitrary order.
Target statistics leak information if computed on the full dataset.
CatBoost, an open-source library from Yandex, solves this by building categorical encoding directly into the boosting algorithm.
It uses permutation-driven target statistics that avoid leakage, and an ordered boosting scheme that reduces prediction shift.
The result: you can feed raw categories to the model, get strong baselines with default hyperparameters, and train fast on GPU.
This matters because real-world data is full of categorical columns — customer IDs, product codes, geographic regions — and handling them poorly silently degrades model quality.
CatBoost removes that preprocessing burden and gives you a robust, production-ready GBDT implementation.
CatBoost is a gradient boosting library that builds an ensemble of oblivious (symmetric) decision trees.
In a standard tree, each node can split on a different feature.
In an oblivious tree, the same split criterion (feature and threshold) is applied at every node at a given depth.
A tree of depth d has exactly 2^d leaves.
This symmetry makes inference fast: you can evaluate the tree by indexing into a flat array of leaf values based on binary decisions at each level.
Classical target statistics (TS) replace a category with the mean target value for that category.
The problem: if you compute TS on the full dataset, the model sees the target for the same row it's predicting, causing target leakage.
CatBoost's Ordered TS avoids this by using a random permutation of the dataset.
For each object j, the TS for a category is computed only from objects that appear before j in the permutation.

The formula is: TS_v = (sum_{i in D_k, before j} y_i + a * p) / (count_{i in D_k, before j} + a) where D_k is the set of objects with that category, 'before j' restricts to preceding objects in the permutation, a is a smoothing parameter, and p is the global average target.
This ensures no object's own target is used to encode its own category.
Ordered Boosting addresses prediction shift — a bias that arises in standard boosting because the gradient for a training example is estimated using the model that was trained on that same example.
CatBoost uses the same random permutation from Ordered TS.
For each step, it maintains a separate model for each prefix of the permutation, and the gradient for object j is computed using the model trained only on objects before j.
This reduces overfitting and improves generalization, though it increases training cost.
Failure mode: Ordered TS and Ordered Boosting rely on random permutations.
If the permutation is not truly random or if the dataset has a temporal structure, the permutation can break that structure.
For time-series data, you should use the `cat_features` parameter carefully and consider using a custom permutation that respects time order.
Another caveat: oblivious trees are less flexible than asymmetric trees.
If your data requires highly asymmetric interactions — where different branches need very different splits — CatBoost may underperform XGBoost or LightGBM.
Also, the smoothing parameter a in TS must be tuned; too small and you overfit to rare categories, too large and you lose signal.
In practice, CatBoost's defaults are strong.
You can often get a good model without hyperparameter tuning.
The library supports GPU training, which significantly speeds up experiments on large datasets.

For very large datasets that don't fit in memory, a common approach is to fit a CatBoost model on a representative sample using the Python API, then apply it to the full dataset via a distributed framework like Spark.
CatBoost handles categorical features natively via Ordered TS, which uses random permutations to avoid target leakage.
Ordered Boosting reduces prediction shift by computing gradients using models trained only on preceding objects in a permutation.
CatBoost builds oblivious (symmetric) trees, which make inference fast but can be less flexible than asymmetric trees for highly uneven interactions.
Use CatBoost when you have many categorical features or want a strong default baseline; consider XGBoost/LightGBM if you need asymmetric tree structures.
For time-series data, be careful with the permutation — you may need to control it to respect temporal order.

# CatBoost

## Definition
CatBoost is a gradient boosting library that builds an ensemble of oblivious decision trees. It is distinguished by native handling of categorical features without manual preprocessing, using ordered target statistics with permutations to avoid target leakage, and employs an ordered boosting mechanism to reduce overfitting.

## Intuition
Traditional GBDT requires conversion of categorical features to numerical ones (one-hot, label encoding), which can cause combinatorial explosion or introduce arbitrary ordering. CatBoost encodes categories by computing target statistics: replacing a category with the mean target (or a smoothed variant) conditioned on that category. To prevent data leakage from using the same target to encode and predict, CatBoost uses permutations and lag-exclusion, encoding each instance using only past data within a random ordering. This yields a powerful, yet leakage-free, representation of categorical variables.

## Mathematical Formulation
Standard gradient boosting objective: add tree f_t to minimize sum L(y_i, F_{t-1}(x_i) + f_t(x_i)) + Omega(f_t). CatBoost uses oblivious trees, where the same splitting criterion and the same feature-threshold pair are applied to all nodes at a given depth. A tree of depth d has 2^d leaves.

For categorical feature k with value v, the ordered target statistic is:
TS_{v} = (sum_{i in D_k, before j} y_i + a * p) / (count_{i in D_k, before j} + a)
where j is the index in a random permutation, D_k is the set of objects with that category, “before j” restricts to preceding objects in the permutation, a is a smoothing strength, and p is the global average target. This ensures that the target for object j is encoded only using data preceding it.

The oblivious tree structure enables evaluation via flat index from binary features, making inference extremely fast.

## When to Use / Not Use
Use CatBoost when the data contains many categorical features, when quick strong baselines are needed, or when avoiding manual one-hot encoding. Excellent for competitions and production due to default robustness. Not ideal if the tree depth needs to model highly asymmetric interactions (consider XGBoost/LightGBM with asymmetric trees), or when domain-specific encoding already exists and is superior. Inference speed benefit of oblivious trees diminishes if extremely deep trees are required.

## Variants / Extensions
CatBoost for ranking (YetiRank, PairLogit), multitask regression, survival analysis. Integration with scikit-learn API. Text feature embeddings via transformers. Other GBDT libraries: LightGBM (leaf‑wise growth, gradient-based one-side sampling), XGBoost (level‑wise, regularized).

## Minimal Example (Python)
```python
from catboost import CatBoostClassifier
X = [['cat', 1], ['dog', 2], ['cat', 3], ['dog', 1]]
y = [0, 1, 0, 1]
model = CatBoostClassifier(iterations=10, depth=2, verbose=0,
                           cat_features=[0])
model.fit(X, y)
print(model.predict([['cat', 2]]))
```

to Use / Not Use
Use for structured/tabular data where predictive accuracy is paramount, for competitions, and when feature importance insights are desired. Not use when model interpretability is critical (white-box decisions), when the dataset is tiny, or when testing with extreme input values outside observed ranges.

## Variants / Extensions
LightGBM (gradient-based one-side sampling, leaf-wise growth), CatBoost (ordered boosting, symmetric trees), XGBoost for ranking, monotonic constraints, GPU-accelerated training, and DART (dropouts in boosting).

## Estimation
A sequence of random permutations is drawn. For each permutation, target statistics are computed with per-instance leave-out. Trees are built greedily using these statistics and gradients. Hyperparameters: iterations, learning_rate, depth (tree depth; number of leaves = 2^depth), l2_leaf_reg, random_strength (amount of randomness in scoring splits), bagging_temperature, and one_hot_max_size for categories. Early stopping by validation set is recommended.

## Assumptions
The boosted model is an additive expansion of trees. The approximation with gradient descent is suitable; loss is differentiable. Categorical features contain meaningful signal exploitable via target encoding. No scaling or distributional assumptions on numeric features; missing values are handled by treating them as a special category or value.

## Key Properties
Top-tier predictive performance with minimal hyperparameter tuning (defaults work well). Native categorical feature handling reduces feature engineering. Ordered TS encoding effectively combats overfitting due to target leakage. Oblivious trees make inference fast and model size small. Built-in support for text features (since version 0.19). Provides feature importance and supports GPU training.

## Failure Modes
When target encoding for a category has too few observations, estimates are noisy; smoothing mitigates but does not eliminate. Oblivious trees may struggle to capture complex interactions that require different splits across nodes at same depth, limiting expressiveness relative to asymmetric trees. Very large number of categorical features can make permutation-based encoding memory intensive. With many iterations, overfitting still occurs if not stopped early.

# XGBoost

## Definition
XGBoost (eXtreme Gradient Boosting) is a scalable machine learning framework that builds an ensemble of regression trees via gradient boosting. It uses second-order Taylor approximation of the loss function, explicit regularization, and system optimizations to achieve high performance and speed.

## Intuition
Trees are added sequentially; each new tree is trained to reduce the residual error of the current ensemble. Instead of fitting raw residuals, XGBoost fits the gradient and curvature of the loss, enabling custom loss functions and faster convergence. Complexity penalties on number of leaves and leaf weights prevent overfitting, while shrinkage (learning rate) makes boosting more robust.

## Mathematical Formulation
The t-th tree f_t is chosen to minimize an objective function at step t:

Obj = sum_i L(y_i, y_hat_i^(t-1) + f_t(x_i)) + Omega(f_t)

L is approximated via second-order Taylor expansion around y_hat^(t-1):

L(y_i, y_hat^(t-1) + f_t(x_i)) ≈ L(y_i, y_hat^(t-1)) + g_i f_t(x_i) + 0.5 h_i [f_t(x_i)]^2

where g_i = ∂L/∂y_hat and h_i = ∂²L/∂y_hat² (gradient and hessian). Regularization Omega(f_t) = gamma T + 0.5 lambda ||w||², with T leaves and leaf weights w.

For a fixed tree structure, optimal leaf weight for leaf j:

w_j* = - (sum_{i in leaf j} g_i) / (sum_{i in leaf j} h_i + lambda)

The resulting optimal objective reduction (split gain) is:

Gain = 0.5 [ (G_L)^2/(H_L + lambda) + (G_R)^2/(H_R + lambda
